title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
text:
Why an instruction file?
Most of us meet AI through a chat window: you type a question, the model types an answer. Newer AI tools can do more than answer. Installed on your own computer, they can open the files in a folder you point them to, read your data and scripts, write new scripts, run them, and look at the result. The AI world calls these tools agents. Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Gemini CLI are examples.
Every conversation with an AI model starts from a blank slate. The model has no memory of your last session, your research group, or the rules you work by, so you end up repeating the same background every time. An instruction file solves this. It is a plain text file with your standing instructions, and the agent reads it automatically at the start of every session, as if you had pasted it in as the first message. Think of it as a starting prompt that you write once.
This page proposes a CHEAC standard instruction file: a short list of rules built on the CHEAC Data Management Plan (Center for High Entropy Alloy Catalysis 2026). We suggest that you copy it into your own instruction file and adapt it to your work.






NoteThis is advisory



The council suggests these rules as a starting point. Adapt them to your own work, and share your experience via the contributing page.

title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
text:
A few terms first
Chat. The web page you open at claude.ai, chatgpt.com, or gemini.google.com. You type, the model answers, and nothing happens outside the browser unless you copy it out yourself.
Agent. A model that can take actions on your computer: open files, edit them, run programs, and read the output, in a loop, until a task is done. You ask “make a plot of the XRD patterns in this folder”, and the agent finds the files, writes a Python script, runs it, looks at the plot, and fixes the script if it fails.
Terminal and CLI. The terminal is a window where you control the computer by typing commands instead of clicking. A program you use this way has a command-line interface (CLI). Most agents are CLI programs. If you have never used a terminal, start with one of these beginner guides:

macOS: Apple’s Terminal User Guide.
Windows: Microsoft’s Windows Terminal overview.
Linux (and a good general introduction): Ubuntu’s The Linux command line for beginners.
Inside VS Code: Getting started with the terminal in VS Code.

Harness. The program wrapped around the model. The model itself only produces text. The harness gives it tools (read a file, run a command, search the web), asks for your permission before risky actions, and loads your instruction file. Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI are harnesses built by the model companies for their own models, and they also come as extensions for the code editor VS Code. Independent harnesses such as OpenCode and OMP work with models from many providers (Stencil Labs 2026).

Account

OpenAI Codex

title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
section: What goes in an instruction file
text:
What goes in an instruction file
An instruction file is a Markdown file: plain text where # marks a heading and - marks a bullet point (Cone 2026). You can write it in any text editor.
Each tool looks for a specific file name. Most tools now read the shared name AGENTS.md, an open format supported by more than twenty tools (Agentic AI Foundation 2025):








Tool
File it reads
Documentation




Claude Code
CLAUDE.md (can also read AGENTS.md)
Anthropic (2026)


OpenAI Codex
AGENTS.md
OpenAI (2026)


Gemini CLI
GEMINI.md
Google (2026)


OpenCode
AGENTS.md (falls back to CLAUDE.md)
OpenCode (2026b)


OMP
AGENTS.md, and the files of the other tools
Stencil Labs (2026)


GitHub Copilot in VS Code
.github/copilot-instructions.md or AGENTS.md
Microsoft (2026)



Files live at two levels:

Global (personal). Applies to everything you do with that tool, for example ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md for Claude Code or ~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md for OpenCode (Anthropic 2026; OpenCode 2026b). The ~ means your home folder.
Project. An AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md) in the top folder of a project. It applies only when the agent works in that folder, and it describes that project: its purpose, its data, and where things are.

The CHEAC rules below ideally belong in your global file, since they apply to all your work. Project details go in the project file.






NoteShort and specific works best



A study of AI coding agents on real software projects found that an AGENTS.md file cut the agents’ median runtime by about 29 % and the text they produced by about 17 %, with the same rate of completed tasks (Lulla et al. 2026). The Claude Code documentation notes that the more concise and specific the file, the more consistently the model follows it (Anthropic 2026, 2025).








WarningInstructions are requests, permissions are locks



The model reads the instruction file as advice and can still get it wrong. Actions that must never happen, such as deleting raw data, also belong in the tool’s permission settings. OpenCode, for example, marks every command as allow, ask, or deny (OpenCode 2026a). A sensible start is to deny deleting files, keep everything else on ask, and move commands to allow once you trust them. Claude Code has the same idea in its permission settings.

title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
text:
Setting it up

Install one agent (see Installing an agent).
Create the global instruction file for that tool (see the table above).
Paste in the CHEAC standard below and fill in the About me section.
For each research project, add a short AGENTS.md in the project folder that describes the project, the same way the DMP asks for a top-level README.
Start a session and ask the agent: “Summarise the instructions you have been given.” It should list your rules back to you.







ImportantLet the agent edit the file for you



The instruction file is an ordinary text file, so your agent can edit it. Ask it directly: “Add a rule to my instruction file that all figures use 300 dpi”, or “Make my AGENTS.md shorter and clearer”. Read the change before you accept it.

title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
text:
The  standard instruction file
Copy the block below with the copy button in its top right corner. The rules follow the C-L-E-A-R standard and the FAIR principles in the DMP (Center for High Entropy Alloy Catalysis 2026; Wilkinson et al. 2016).
# CHEAC agent instructions (v1, September 2026)

## About me
- I am a researcher at the Center for High Entropy Alloy Catalysis (CHEAC),
  University of Copenhagen / University of Bern. My field: <fill in>.

## Research data (follows the CHEAC Data Management Plan)
- Never modify, move, rename, or delete raw data: instrument output,
  simulation output, or files from external facilities. Treat them as
  read-only.
- Write processed data to a separate, clearly labelled folder
  (e.g. `processed/`), never next to the raw file under a similar name.
- Every project folder has a top-level README; every dataset folder has its
  own README with instrument or software version, parameters, date,
  responsible researcher, and purpose. Offer to create or update these when
  you add data or scripts.
- Save every analysis and figure script in the same folder as the data it
  uses. A published figure must be reproducible from that folder alone.
- Prefer plain text and open formats (CSV, JSON, Python scripts) over
  binary or proprietary formats.
- Record software versions and random seeds in scripts and READMEs.
- Do not upload data to any external service without my approval.

## Scientific integrity
- Never invent data, numbers, references, or DOIs. If you do not know,
  say so.
- Every literature claim needs a source I can check. Give the DOI or URL.
- State units, uncertainties, and assumptions explicitly.
- When a result looks surprising, say so and suggest how to check it
  before I rely on it.

## Code
- Keep scripts short, commented, and runnable from the command line.
- Ask before installing packages or changing my software environment.

## Actions that need my approval
- Deleting or overwriting any file.
- Copying data off my machine (SFTP, cloud upload, git push).
- Anything involving passwords, keys, or login details. Never print them.

## When you finish a task
- Summarise what you changed, which files you created, and anything I
  should check by hand.
Add your own habits to the Code section, such as your preferred programming language and plotting style. Keep the file short: every line competes for the model’s attention.

title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
section: Using it in the web chat
text:
Using it in the web chat
The same text works as a starting prompt in the web chat versions. There the model cannot touch your files, but the rules still shape its answers:

Claude: create a Project and paste the rules into its instructions.
ChatGPT: paste the rules into the custom instructions in your settings, or into the instructions of a project.
Gemini: create a Gem with the rules as its instructions.
Any chat: paste the rules as your first message.

The Scientific integrity section matters in chat as much as in an agent.

title: A  standard for AI agent instructions
section: Skills: a topic for another time
text:
Skills: a topic for another time
Instruction files hold rules that apply to everything. Skills hold know-how for one kind of task, such as “how to write a README for a new dataset”, “how to make a publication-quality figure”, or “how to check a reference list”. A skill is a folder with a Markdown file of instructions and optional scripts, and the agent loads it only when the task calls for it (Agent Skills 2025). Skills deserve their own post. Until then, see agentskills.io and Anthropic’s introduction to skills.

title: Contributing
text:
Adding a page
Place a new .qmd (or .md) file in the folder of its section:



Section
Folder




Best Practices
practices/


Guidelines
guidelines/


AI in research
ai-in-research/


Transparency
transparency/


AI News
news/



A page can also live in its own subfolder, for example news/my-story/index.qmd, next to its figures.
The section list, the navbar link, and the Most recent list on the front page pick up new pages automatically. They read the header at the top of the file:
---
title: "Short, descriptive title"
author:
  - name: Your Name
    affiliation: "Position, Group"
date: 2026-10-01
description: "One sentence shown under the title in the section list."
image: ../assets/figures/my-figure.svg   # optional cover figure
---

title is required. Without it, the page appears in the lists without a name.
date places the page in the lists. Pages without a date sort as the oldest and do not appear under Most recent.
image sets the cover figure in the section list. Without it, the list uses the first image on the page, or none.

title: KU guidelines on AI usage
text:
1. AI use by employees
The employee guide (found in KUnet) is the most relevant starting point for staff. It includes rules for using AI tools, guidance on choosing tools, and instructions for accessing them securely.

Copilot Chat is KU’s approved AI tool and must be used when handling the personal data covered by the guidance. This includes employee names, KU email addresses, education and employment details, job titles, areas of work, organisational affiliations and work phone numbers. You must be signed in with your KU account when entering this information.
Other AI tools may be used where there are significant teaching or research reasons for choosing them. According to the guidelines, confidential, personal or copyrighted data must not be entered into these alternative tools.
Although much of our research in  does not involve personal data, these rules may be relevant to consider for administrative tasks, or when sharing working files with an AI agent.
The guide includes instructions for securely accessing and using Copilot Chat, and for assessing the security of alternative tools.

KU employee guide: AI

title: KU guidelines on AI usage
text:
2. AI use in PhD theses
KU permits appropriate use of AI-assisted technologies, provided students carefully check the output and ensure that their use does not compromise the requirements for a PhD.
The main points are:

Verify all facts and references. AI has a habit of confidently inventing information and publications. Never include any information provided to you that you cannot verify.
Limit the freedom given to generative AI. KU recommends limiting the freedom of generative AI by giving specific and appropriate prompts - don’t just provide blocks of text and ask for general improvements.
Disclose and describe AI use clearly. An exhaustive account of prompts and responses is not necessary, but it is necessary to describe how you have used AI. Analytical AI tools should be described or referenced like other analytical software.
AI cannot be listed as a co-author. You remain responsible for the accuracy, integrity and originality of the entire work, including any errors or plagiarism.

KU guidance: AI-assisted technologies in PhD theses

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
Concerning folders
A couple of weeks before handing in his thesis, Sam needs to update Figure 3. His supervisor wants to see the cyclic voltammograms before the latest corrections, because “the peaks looked nicer in that version”.
Fair enough. The problem is finding it.
HEA_CVs/
├── plot_cv.py
├── plot_cv_new.py
├── plot_cv_new_FINAL.py
├── plot_cv_new_FINAL_v2_after_meeting.py
├── plot_cv_new_FINAL_v2_after_meeting_REALLY.py
├── fig3.png
├── fig3_new.png
├── fig3_new_new.png
└── HEA17_CV_C01.mpr
Which script produced fig3_new.png? Does FINAL include the iR correction? Was the electrode area changed before or after that meeting? Sam can work it out, probably, but it’ll take an afternoon that could have been spent on the thesis.
Most of us have made some version of this folder. It’s an understandable way to work: when a script finally produces a good figure, you make a copy before touching it again. Then another copy. Before long, the filenames are doing a very bad job of recording your decisions.
Git lets you keep one working copy of the script while saving its history. You can see what changed, recover an older version, and try something new without making another FINAL_v2_REALLY.py. It also makes working with co-authors and AI coding agents considerably less chaotic.
We’ll follow Sam’s BioLogic data from the first plotting script to the version submitted with the paper. The point isn’t to turn everyone into a software developer. It’s to make it easy to answer a very ordinary research question: what exactly did I do to make this figure?
Thanks to Till Schertenleib for suggesting the topic in the Suggestion box.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
A long-expected commit
Git records versions of files. Each saved version is called a commit: a snapshot of the files you chose, together with a short message about what you changed. You decide when to make one. Git doesn’t save every keystroke.
That gives you two things a folder full of copies doesn’t: a history you can inspect, and a way to move between versions without keeping them all on your desktop.

Git is not GitHub
These two are often mentioned together, but they’re different things:

Git runs on your computer. It keeps the history, even without an internet connection or an account.
GitHub hosts a copy of a git repository online. It’s useful for sharing code, reviewing changes, and keeping another copy somewhere other than your laptop.

You can use git without GitHub. We’ll start there and add GitHub once we have something worth sharing.


Install git

Windows: Install it from git-scm.com. The default settings are fine. The installer also includes Git Bash, where the commands below will work.
macOS: Open Terminal and run git --version. If git isn’t installed, macOS should offer to install the command-line tools.
Linux: On Ubuntu, run sudo apt install git. Other distributions have equivalent packages.

Check that it works:
git --version
Then set the name and email that will appear next to your commits (once per computer):
git config --global user.name "Sam Gamgee"
git config --global user.email "sam@chem.ku.dk"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
Use your own name and email, of course. The last line tells git to call the initial branch main.






NoteDon’t like terminals?



GitHub Desktop and VS Code’s Source Control panel let you do most of this with buttons. They’re perfectly good ways to use git. I’ll show commands because they’re easy to copy and work across operating systems.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
The fellowship of the folder
Before using git, Sam cleans up the project. The CHEAC Data Management Plan already has a sensible approach: explain the project in a README, keep the original measurements untouched, and separate data, scripts, and figures.
Let’s give the CV analysis a home:
hea17-orr/
├── README.md              # what this project does and where the data is stored
├── .gitignore             # files git should leave alone
├── requirements.txt       # Python packages used for the analysis
├── data/
│   ├── raw/               # original BioLogic files, kept outside git
│   └── processed/         # smaller files produced during analysis
├── scripts/
│   └── plot_cv.py
└── figures/
    └── fig3_cv.png
It’s still just an ordinary folder. Git doesn’t require a particular structure, but it helps if the folder makes sense before you start recording its history.

What should git keep?
Git works best with text files: Python scripts, notebooks, READMEs, configuration files, and reasonably small tables. Large binary files, especially ones that change often, can make a repository unnecessarily large.
For this project, we’ll keep the code and small analysis files in git, but leave the original .mpr measurements in the lab’s data storage on ASIMOV or ERDA. Sam creates a file called .gitignore:
# Original measurements are archived separately
data/raw/
*.mpr
.env

# Temporary Python and notebook files
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
The README should say exactly where to find the raw files, which measurements were used, and how to run the analysis. It’s fine to have a local data/raw/ folder containing copies of those files; git simply won’t include them in commits.
This distinction matters. Git keeps a history of your code, not a complete record of your experiment. Reproducing a figure also requires the right raw measurements, calibration values, metadata, and software environment. That’s why we keep requirements.txt alongside the script and archive the raw data separately.
GitHub has ready-made .gitignore examples for common languages and tools. When your Python environment is working, you can record the installed versions with python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt (ideally from an environment made just for this project).






WarningKeep credentials out of git



Passwords, access tokens, SSH keys, and anything else you wouldn’t want to publish should stay out of the repository. Put local credentials in a separate ignored file or an environment variable. Deleting a secret from a script later does not remove it from git’s history.




Your first commit
Open a terminal in the project folder:
cd hea17-orr
git init
git status
git init creates the repository. git status shows what’s currently going on. Before the first commit, you’ll see something like:
On branch main
No commits yet

Untracked files:
  .gitignore
  README.md
  requirements.txt
  scripts/
Notice that data/raw/ isn’t listed. That’s because we told git to ignore it. Empty folders won’t show up either: git tracks files, not folders on their own.
Now save the first version:
git add .gitignore README.md requirements.txt scripts/
git commit -m "Add initial HEA17 CV plotting script"
git add chooses what goes into the next commit. git commit saves that version, and the text after -m is your note to your future self.
That’s the basic idea. No GitHub account, no special project setup, and no more copying scripts to keep the old versions.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
The road goes ever on
Here’s a shortened version of Sam’s plotting script. It uses ixdat to load BioLogic measurements and plot the third CV cycle:
# scripts/plot_cv.py
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from ixdat import Measurement

raw = Path("data/raw")
files = sorted(raw.glob("HEA17_CV_*.mpr"))
if not files:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No HEA17 CV files found in data/raw/")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
for path in files:
    cv = Measurement.read(path, reader="biologic").as_cv()
    cv.calibrate_RE(RE_vs_RHE=0.92)  # V, from the RHE calibration
    cv[3].plot_vs_potential(ax=ax, label=path.stem)

ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=7)
Path("figures").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
fig.savefig("figures/fig3_cv.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")
Run it from the project folder with python scripts/plot_cv.py. To install the packages used here:
python -m pip install ixdat matplotlib galvani
The galvani package is needed for ixdat to read many BioLogic .mpr files. If yours doesn’t load, ixdat can also use eclabfiles, or you can export an .mpt text file from EC-Lab. The ixdat documentation covers the different readers, including working with ASIMOV.
Keep requirements.txt updated when you change your Python packages. Together with the raw-data location, calibration values, and script, it gives someone else in the group a much better chance of reproducing the figure.

The everyday workflow
A week later, Sam gets an impedance measurement and wants to add iR correction. The workflow is simple: edit, check, commit.
After adding the correction, run:
git diff
Git shows the difference between the working file and the last saved version:
     cv.calibrate_RE(RE_vs_RHE=0.92)  # V, from the RHE calibration
+    cv.correct_ohmic_drop(R_Ohm=45)  # ohm, from EIS
     cv[3].plot_vs_potential(ax=ax, label=path.stem)
A + means a line was added; a - means it was removed. Nothing mysterious happened here. Sam added the correction, checked that the change was what he intended, and saves it:
git add scripts/plot_cv.py
git commit -m "Add iR correction using 45 ohm from EIS"
That’s most of what you need to do on a normal day. You don’t have to commit every time you press Run. Commit when you’ve made a change you’d want to understand or recover later.


Commit messages are for future you
A useful message says what changed and, when it isn’t obvious, why. Compare these:



Not very helpful
Much better




update
Use cycle 3; earlier cycles still show oxide reduction


fix
Add iR correction using 45 ohm from EIS


new fig
Compare HEA17 and Pt reference in Fig. 3


asdf
Normalise current by geometric area (0.196 cm²)



Try to keep each commit about one thing. A change to the reference-electrode calibration and a change to the plot colours don’t need to be in the same commit.
You can see the history at any point:
git log --oneline
e41f0a2 Compare HEA17 and Pt reference in Fig. 3
9c3d7b1 Normalise current by geometric area (0.196 cm²)
5b2a8e4 Add iR correction using 45 ohm from EIS
a1b2c3d Add initial HEA17 CV plotting script
Each line is a commit. The short string on the left, such as 5b2a8e4, identifies the version. That’s what you’ll use when someone asks about the figure from two weeks ago.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
The shadow of the past
And, sure enough, Sam’s supervisor does. They want to compare the latest CV with the version before area normalisation.
The good news is that Sam doesn’t have to guess which backup script was used. Git already knows. There are a few ways to go back, depending on what you want.
Undo a change you haven’t committed. Say you’ve been editing plot_cv.py, it no longer runs, and you’d rather return to your last commit:
git restore scripts/plot_cv.py
This discards the uncommitted edits in that file. Check git diff first if you’re unsure.
Get one file from an older commit. To run the version before area normalisation:
git restore --source=5b2a8e4 scripts/plot_cv.py
python scripts/plot_cv.py
Now Sam can regenerate the older figure with the same raw measurements. The old code is a temporary change in the working folder; the commit history hasn’t moved. When he’s finished comparing, he can restore the latest committed script:
git restore scripts/plot_cv.py
Be careful with the figure itself: the script may overwrite figures/fig3_cv.png. Save the comparison under a different name if you want both copies. And if you later reproduce a much older analysis, remember that the Python environment and raw-data versions may matter too.
Visit an older version of the entire project. First commit or set aside any work you want to keep. Then:
git switch --detach 5b2a8e4
# inspect files or run the old analysis
git switch main
Git calls this detached HEAD. The name sounds worse than it is. You’re looking at a particular commit instead of working on a branch. git switch main gets you back.
Reverse a commit without erasing the history. If the area normalisation turns out to have used the wrong electrode area:
git revert 9c3d7b1
Git makes a new commit that undoes that change. You can still see both the mistake and the correction, much like in a proper lab notebook.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
Side quests: branches
Now Sam wants to try a different baseline correction. It might reveal a small oxidation peak. Or it might just make the plot worse.
This is where branches are handy. A branch is a separate line of commits. You can try something without changing the version you’re currently happy with.
Start with a clean working folder, then:
git switch -c try-baseline
# edit and test the script
git add scripts/plot_cv.py
git commit -m "Try linear baseline between 0.05 and 0.25 V"
The main branch, main, is still where you left it.
If the idea works, bring it back:
git switch main
git merge try-baseline
git branch -d try-baseline
If it doesn’t, leave it behind:
git switch main
git branch -D try-baseline
The capital -D forces deletion even though the experiment wasn’t merged, so only use it when you’re happy to discard the branch. You can also simply keep the branch around until you’ve decided.
Either way, there’s no need for plot_cv_baseline_TEST_dont_use.py.






NoteWhat about merge conflicts?



If you changed the same lines on main and on your branch, git may need you to choose which edit to keep. It marks the disagreement in the file:
<<<<<<< HEAD
    cv.correct_ohmic_drop(R_Ohm=45)
=======
    cv.correct_ohmic_drop(R_Ohm=47)  # re-measured
>>>>>>> try-baseline
Edit the file to keep the correct value, remove the marker lines, then run git add scripts/plot_cv.py and git commit. It’s annoying the first time, but it’s better than silently losing one person’s correction.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
Git and AI agents
Here’s another situation that’s probably becoming familiar. You ask an AI coding agent to fix a legend. It fixes the legend, but it also renames two variables, reorganises a function, and starts testing a different smoothing window. The new figure looks fine. The problem is that six files changed, and you didn’t ask for most of it.
Git makes these changes much easier to deal with, because you can inspect what the agent actually did rather than relying on its description.
My rules are fairly simple:

Commit your own work before starting. If the agent makes a mess, you have a known-good version to return to. Check git status first; git restore . only discards unstaged changes to tracked files, not new untracked files or staged changes.
Use a branch for larger experiments. Let the agent try a new smoothing method on try-smoothing, not on the version you’re preparing for the paper.
Ask for small, focused changes. Fix the legend, check the plot, commit. Then decide whether to do anything else.
Read git diff yourself. An agent’s summary can miss things. The diff tells you which lines really changed.
Don’t let the agent decide what to investigate next. If it suggests another analysis, ask what question that analysis would answer. A plausible-sounding side quest is still a side quest.

The same habits are useful when you’re writing code yourself, but they’re especially valuable with agents because they can change a lot of code very quickly.
If you use an instruction file (see A CHEAC standard for AI agent instructions), you can put the rules there. For example, add this to AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md:
## Git
- Check `git status` before editing. If I have uncommitted work, don't
  overwrite it or make a commit without asking me.
- Use a separate branch for experiments; don't modify `main` without asking.
- Keep changes focused. Make small commits with messages saying what changed.
- Never commit raw measurements, credentials, tokens, or other ignored files.
- Show me the diff before treating a task as finished.
- Ask before merging, rebasing, pushing, force-pushing, or deleting branches.
- Don't suggest additional analyses unless you can explain what question
  they would answer.
One important detail: don’t give an agent blanket permission to run destructive git commands. In particular, git restore, git reset --hard, and git clean can wipe out work that hasn’t been committed. Make sure you know what’s about to be discarded.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
The fellowship: GitHub and co-authors
Until now, the repository has lived entirely on Sam’s laptop. That works, but it’s risky. If the laptop disappears, the local git history goes with it.
Time to put a copy online. GitHub is convenient, although it doesn’t replace the group’s proper data storage and backup arrangements.

Create an account at github.com.
Install the GitHub CLI and log in:
gh auth login
In the project folder, create a private repository and push the existing history:
gh repo create hea17-orr --private --source=. --remote=origin --push

After that, the usual commands are:
git push    # send your commits to GitHub
git pull    # bring in commits from GitHub
Start private, especially if the project contains unpublished work. Before making it public, check what you’ve committed, whether you have permission to share it, and whether the repository contains data or information that should stay internal.

Working with co-authors
Merry is working on the DFT part of the paper and wants to change the plotting script. Rather than emailing an edited file to Sam, Merry makes a branch and opens a pull request on GitHub.
A pull request is just a proposed change. Sam can look through the diff, comment on individual lines, ask Merry to adjust things, and merge it into main when they’re both happy. It’s a particularly nice way to review changes to analysis scripts without having to compare two attachments called final.py.
This website is updated through pull requests too.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
There and back again
The paper is ready. The figures have been checked, the scripts are committed, and the raw data is stored where the group expects it. A few final steps make it easier to return to the submitted version later.

Mark the version you submitted
A tag gives a particular commit a name. Sam tags the version used for submission:
git tag -a v1.0-submitted -m "Version submitted to ACS Catalysis"
git push origin v1.0-submitted
When Reviewer 2 asks for another control experiment, Sam can do the revision work as usual and later tag v1.1-revision. The original submission stays easy to find.


Archive the code alongside the data
Git can package the tagged files into a zip:
git archive --format=zip -o hea17-orr-v1.0.zip v1.0-submitted
This contains the tracked files in that commit, not the git history and not the ignored raw measurements. Put it in the ERDA project archive alongside the raw data, relevant metadata, and anything else needed to rerun the analysis. Follow the CHEAC Data Management Plan for the full archiving requirements.
If you need the full git history in the archive as well, archive the repository separately; git archive intentionally makes a clean source snapshot.


Give the code a DOI (optional)
If the code is going to be public, you can connect the GitHub repository to Zenodo, create a GitHub release from the tag, and have Zenodo archive that release with a DOI. GitHub has a guide. It’s an easy way to give readers a specific, citable version rather than a link to a repository that may keep changing.
And that’s it. Sam still has one plotting script in his working folder. The difference is that all the earlier versions are in git, complete with the changes that got him from one to the next.
He can finally delete plot_cv_new_FINAL_v2_after_meeting_REALLY.py.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
When things go wrong
“I accidentally staged something.” Unstage it without deleting the file:
git restore --staged data/processed/results.csv
“I committed a huge raw-data file.” First, stop tracking it and add it to .gitignore:
git rm --cached data/raw/huge_file.mpr
If you added the file in your most recent commit and haven’t pushed, you can amend that commit after updating .gitignore:
git add .gitignore
git commit --amend --no-edit
If the file was committed earlier, or has already been pushed, that doesn’t remove it from the old history. Cleaning the history takes extra steps and may affect collaborators. Get help before rewriting a shared repository’s history.
“I committed a password or token.” Revoke or rotate it immediately. Even if you remove it from your latest file, the old value may still be accessible in the history.
“Git says detached HEAD.” You’re looking at an old commit. If you’ve only been inspecting things, git switch main takes you back. If you’ve made commits there that you want to keep, make a branch before switching.
“I broke the script and want the last committed version back.” Check what you’re throwing away with git diff, then:
git restore scripts/plot_cv.py
For everything else, Oh Shit, Git!?! is a very good collection of solutions to common git disasters.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
Cheat sheet







What you want to do
Command




Start a repository
git init


Check what’s changed
git status


See edits line by line
git diff


Stage a file
git add <file>


Unstage a file
git restore --staged <file>


Save a version
git commit -m "What changed"


See past versions
git log --oneline


Discard uncommitted edits to a tracked file
git restore <file>


Get a file from an old commit
git restore --source=<commit> <file>


Visit an old commit
git switch --detach <commit>


Return to main
git switch main


Reverse a commit with a new one
git revert <commit>


Start an experimental branch
git switch -c try-<name>


Merge the experiment
git switch main then git merge try-<name>


Delete a merged branch
git branch -d try-<name>


Force-delete an unmerged branch
git branch -D try-<name>


Send commits to GitHub
git push


Get changes from GitHub
git pull


Tag a version
git tag -a v1.0-submitted -m "..."


Export tagged files as a zip
git archive --format=zip -o out.zip v1.0-submitted



There’s also a printable GitHub cheat sheet.

title: One folder to rule them all: a git workflow for research
text:
Further reading

Software Carpentry: Version Control with Git is written for researchers and includes exercises you can follow.
Pro Git is a free book if you want to understand what happens underneath (Chacon and Straub 2014).
Short introductions to git in research: (Blischak et al. 2016) and (Ram 2013).
Good enough practices in scientific computing is a useful guide to keeping research projects manageable (Wilson et al. 2017).

text:
